content: Reactive drug administration (RDA) involves providing antimalarial medications to individuals living with or near a person with a confirmed malaria infection or to those who were likely exposed to the infection at the same time and place as the index case. The goal of RDA is to treat existing infections and prevent new ones during the post-treatment prophylaxis period of the drug. Antimalarial drugs used in RDA, such as artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) or chloroquine, may also include primaquine for radical cure of Plasmodium vivax or a single low dose of primaquine for Plasmodium falciparum to target gametocytes. Reactive interventions should focus on the likely location of infection for the index case, determined through case investigations that consider the date of symptom onset and the parasite’s incubation period. If the likely location of infection is a residence, RDA can be administered to the household of the confirmed case and potentially extended to neighbors. Programs implementing RDA must have the capacity to conduct case investigations at the residence to identify the likely location of infection and co-exposed individuals. They should also enumerate and provide antimalarial medications to people living with or near the confirmed case and others sharing the same risk of infection. The targeted population should include household members, neighbors, co-travelers, and co-workers, depending on the local epidemiology and ecology of malaria. However, if the infection was imported and the residence is not in a receptive area, RDA may not be beneficial. For P. vivax, programs should carefully consider how to safely and feasibly administer treatment to prevent relapses, including testing for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency before treatment. RDA should be part of a broader malaria elimination program, including intensive follow-up of cases and strong passive surveillance systems to detect and investigate suspected cases. Without these elements, RDA is unlikely to impact transmission. High coverage and adherence to antimalarial medications are critical for RDA success. Community engagement is essential to build trust and improve participation and adherence, especially since many asymptomatic individuals may be asked to take medication despite not feeling ill. Antimalarial drugs used in RDA should be WHO-recommended, effective against local parasites, safe, well-tolerated, and cost-effective. Single-dose regimens are preferred for ease of administration and adherence. Reactive case detection and treatment (RACDT) involves testing all individuals living with or near a confirmed malaria case or those likely exposed at the same time and place as the index case. Only those who test positive are treated with a full therapeutic course of antimalarial medication. Unlike RDA, RACDT does not provide population-level prophylaxis but may improve adherence, acceptance, and equity while reducing unintended consequences and preserving medicine stocks. RACDT is particularly useful in areas nearing malaria elimination, as it enhances surveillance sensitivity and identifies additional cases around the index case, revealing gaps in the surveillance system. It also provides evidence for malaria elimination certification by demonstrating zero indigenous cases. RACDT should be implemented according to standardized operating procedures (SOPs) and should include testing and treating all individuals at risk, including household members, neighbors, and co-exposed individuals. Countries with low malaria transmission but not yet close to elimination should prioritize RDA and reactive indoor residual spraying (IRS) over RACDT. However, RACDT can complement RDA in areas closer to elimination to strengthen surveillance and monitor progress. Post-elimination, RACDT can help prevent re-establishment of malaria and support certification of malaria-free status. The evidence for the impact of RDA and RACDT on malaria transmission is limited and of low certainty. While RDA may reduce malaria prevalence and incidence, the benefits and harms of RACDT remain uncertain due to a lack of studies comparing it to no intervention. Both strategies require further research to optimize their implementation, assess their impact, and address potential harms or unintended consequences.
